10:2.headline: A divided heart is what leaves Israel open to blame
10:2.body: Rashi stops on this word to bring a midrash. When Israel served idols but stayed united, no accuser could speak against them. Once their heart was divided, they became guilty.

sources.quote: גָּדוֹל הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עָבְדוּ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְשָׁלוֹם בֵּינֵיהֶם, אֵין הַשָּׂטָן מְקַטְרֵג בֵּינֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi cites a midrash: peace is so great that even when Israel served idols but were at peace, the accuser could not accuse them.

sources.quote: וְשָׂנוּי הַמַּחֲלֹקֶת, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: חָלַק לִבָּם עַתָּה יֶאְשָׁמוּ
sources.says: Rashi says division is hateful, and proves it from "their heart is divided, now they will be guilty".

sources.quote: חלק - כי אין להם חלק אחד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means they are no longer one.

10:2.headline: יאשמו: found guilty, or made desolate?
10:2.body: The word usually means to be guilty, and the Targum reads it that way. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it here as becoming desolate, as in תאשם שמרון later in Hosea.

sources.quote: כְּעַן יְחוֹבוּן
sources.says: The Targum renders it "now they will be guilty".

sources.quote: עתה יאשמו - מגזרת שממה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from the word for desolation.

sources.quote: יאשמו. ענין שממה וכן תאשם שמרון
sources.says: Radak says יאשמו means desolation, as in "Samaria shall be desolate".

sources.quote: בא על חיוב העונש, וגם על קבלת העונש
sources.says: Malbim says it means both being liable to punishment and receiving it.

10:2.headline: The calf's altars get their necks broken, like a calf
10:2.body: יערף is the word for breaking an animal's neck. Rashi ties it to the heifer whose neck is broken in Deuteronomy 21:4. Malbim says the prophet chose it because these altars served the golden calf.

sources.quote: יַשְׁחִית. לְשׁוֹן ״וְעָרְפוּ שָׁם״
sources.says: Rashi says it means destroy, using the word for breaking the heifer's neck in Deuteronomy 21:4.

sources.quote: ועל שהיה המזבח עשוי אל העגל ימליצהו עריפת עגלת בקר
sources.says: Malbim says that because the altar was made for the calf, the prophet pictures it as breaking a heifer's neck.

11:3.headline: A one-time verb form: God taught Ephraim to walk
11:3.body: תרגלתי comes from רגל, foot, and means 'I taught to walk'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra say this form, with ת at the front, appears nowhere else in the Bible.

sources.quote: תִרְגַּלְתִּי. כְּמוֹ ׳הִרְגַּלְתִּי׳, וְאֵין לוֹ דִּמְיוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says it means the same as הרגלתי, 'I trained', and has no parallel.

sources.quote: תי"ו תרגלתי תחת ה"א ואין כמוהו במקרא, והטעם הרגלתיו ללכת על רגליו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the ת stands in place of ה, there is no other word like it in Scripture, and it means 'I taught him to walk on his feet'.

sources.quote: ובזה אמר תרגלתי, נעשיתי רגל לאפרים, דהיינו הדום רגליו
sources.says: Malbim reads it as 'I became a foot for Ephraim', meaning his footstool.

11:4.headline: Jaw or wooden post? Two pictures of the lifted yoke
11:4.body: לחי usually means jaw or cheek. Radak keeps that sense, while Rashi links it to the wooden post at the side of an alley and pictures the yoke lifted with boards.

sources.quote: וְעַל לְחֵיהֶם. לְשׁוֹן לֶחִי שֶׁל מָבוֹי
sources.says: Rashi says the word is the same as the side-post of an alley.

sources.quote: הַמְּרִימִים עֹל בִּידֵיהֶם עַל יְדֵי לְוָחִים לְהָקֵל מֵעַל הַפָּרָה הַחוֹרֶשֶׁת
sources.says: Rashi pictures good farmers lifting the yoke by hand with boards to ease the plowing cow.

sources.quote: ומרימים העול מעל צוארה ותולין אותה על לחיה
sources.says: Radak pictures the yoke lifted off the calf's neck and hung on its jaw so it can rest.

11:6.headline: Not 'fall sick': the sword lands and rests on his cities
11:6.body: וחלה looks like the verb for being sick. Rashi and Radak read it as 'it will fall and rest', the way a curse 'falls on the head of Joab'.

sources.quote: וְחָלָה חֶרֶב. וְתָנוּחַ חֶרֶב בְּעָרָיו
sources.says: Rashi says it means the sword will rest in his cities.

sources.quote: וחלה חרב. תפול ותנוח כמו יחולו על ראש יואב
sources.says: Radak says it means it will fall and rest, as in 'let it fall on the head of Joab'.

11:6.headline: One word with two chant marks, read as its own sentence
11:6.body: This word carries two chant marks at once. Rashi says it is marked that way because it stands alone as a statement: all this comes from their own plans.

sources.quote: נָקוּד שְׁנֵי טְעָמִים, בּוֹ הַטִּפְּחָא בּוֹ הַסִּלּוּק, לְפִי שֶׁהוּא דִּבּוּר בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is marked with two accents, tipcha and silluk, because it is a statement by itself.

sources.quote: וכל זה יבא להם מעצתם הרעה
sources.says: Radak says it means all this will come on them from their own bad advice.

11:7.headline: Returning to God, or turning away from him?
11:7.body: Rashi reads למשובתי as 'returning to me': the people waver over whether to repent. Ibn Ezra and Radak object that this word always means rebellion, so the verse is about turning away.

sources.quote: תְלוּאִים הֵם אִם לָשׁוּב אִם לֹא לָשׁוּב
sources.says: Rashi says that when the prophets teach them to return, they hang undecided whether to return or not.

sources.quote: כי משובה לעולם לגנאי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word משובה is always used in a bad sense.

sources.quote: ולא מצאנו משובה כי אם לגנאי
sources.says: Radak notes Rashi's reading as repentance, but says משובה is found only in a bad sense.

11:7.headline: Here על, usually 'on', means 'the Most High'
11:7.body: על is normally the small word for 'on' or 'over'. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read it here as a name for God, 'the One on high'.

sources.quote: ואל על - כמו: נאם הגבר הוקם על שהוא תואר כמו עליון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says על here is a description meaning 'most high', as in 'the man raised on high'.

sources.quote: על. מל׳ עליון וכן על עולה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says על comes from עליון, 'most high'.

11:8.headline: God's pity grows hot, a word Rashi calls Aramaic
11:8.body: נכמרו means 'grew warm', said of strong pity, as skin 'burns like an oven' in Lamentations. Rashi calls it an Aramaic word, while Radak prefers 'rolled over', following the Targum.

sources.quote: נִתְחַמְּמוּ, לְשׁוֹן אֲרַמִּי, וְכֵן ״עוֹרֵנוּ כְּתַנּוּר נִכְמָרוּ״
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'grew hot', calls it Aramaic, and compares 'our skin burns like an oven'.

sources.quote: נתגלגלו נחומי שאני ניחם על הרעה
sources.says: Radak says it means 'my regrets rolled over', that God relents from the harm he planned.

12:1.headline: Judah still 'rules' with God, or still holds close to God
12:1.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read רד as 'rules', so Judah still governs in the fear of God. Malbim adds that it may come from a root meaning 'to join', so Judah is still bound to God.

sources.quote: מוֹשֵׁל עוֹד בְּיִרְאַת אֱלֹהִים
sources.says: Rashi says Judah still rules in the fear of God.

sources.quote: ענין ממשלה כמו רדה בקרב אויביך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means rule, as in 'rule among your enemies'.

sources.quote: וי"ל ששרשו רדד מענין חיבור
sources.says: Malbim says it means rule, or it may come from a root meaning joining.

12:2.headline: Ephraim 'grazes on wind', or makes friends with it
12:2.body: רעה can mean to graze or to befriend. Radak says Ephraim is like someone who opens his mouth to feed on the wind, while Rashi reads it as joining himself to the empty words of idol worship.

sources.quote: דומה למי שפותח פיו אל הרוח ורועה אותו
sources.says: Radak says worshipping the calves is like opening your mouth to the wind to feed on it.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן ׳רֵיעַ׳, מִתְחַבֵּר לְדִבְרֵי רוּחַ
sources.says: Rashi says it comes from the word for friend: he attaches himself to empty words.

sources.quote: הוא מרעה את הרוח ר״ל עוסק הוא בדברי הבל
sources.says: Metzudat David says he herds the wind, meaning he busies himself with nonsense.

12:4.headline: Jacob grabbed the heel, and the heel means 'the end'
12:4.body: עקב, 'he held the heel', is the act behind the name יעקב. Radak adds that the heel is the end of the foot, a sign that in the end Jacob's children would rule over Esau's.

sources.quote: כי בסוף והוא העקב ישלטו בני יעקב בבני עשו
sources.says: Radak says the heel stands for the end: at the end of days Jacob's children will rule Esau's.

sources.quote: אָחֲזוֹ בְּעַקֵבוֹ סִימָן שֶׁהוּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ גְּבִיר
sources.says: Rashi says holding the heel was a sign Jacob would be master over his brother.

sources.quote: שם יעקב, שברח ע"י העקב שעקב את אחיו
sources.says: Malbim ties the name Jacob to the heel, 'he heeled his brother'.

12:4.headline: 'He strove with God': the root of the name Israel
12:4.body: שרה means he struggled and prevailed, from a word for being a prince or ruler. Radak, quoting his father, ties it to the name ישראל: 'you have striven with God and with men and prevailed'.

sources.quote: שרה. מלשון שררה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שרה comes from the word for rule.

sources.quote: ובכחו נעשה שר אל אלהים הוא המלאך שרו של עשו
sources.says: Metzudat David says by his strength Jacob became a prince over the angel, Esau's guardian angel.

sources.quote: ולקרא שמך ישראל לאמר כי שרית עם אלהים ועם אנשים ותוכל
sources.says: Radak quotes his father's reading that God would name him Israel, saying 'you have striven with God and men and prevailed'.

12:5.headline: Who wept? Hosea adds tears the Torah never mentions
12:5.body: Genesis says nothing about weeping in Jacob's fight. Rashi and Radak say it was the angel who wept and begged to be let go.

sources.quote: בָּכָה. הַמַּלְאָךְ
sources.says: Rashi says the one who wept was the angel.

sources.quote: זה לא נזכר בתורה ופי' כאלו המלאך בכה והתחנן ליעקב שישלחנו
sources.says: Radak says this is not in the Torah, and explains it as the angel weeping and begging Jacob to release him.

sources.quote: המלאך וכמעט בכה ויתחנן לו שישלחנו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the angel nearly wept as he pleaded to be let go.

12:6.headline: Why God's 'remembrance' and not God's 'name'
12:6.body: The verse says ה' זכרו, 'the LORD is His remembrance'. Malbim says a שם is a name for what one is, while a זכר is the name one earns through deeds, as in 'this is My name forever and this My remembrance'.

sources.quote: וזכר השם הוא השם העצמי, והזכר הוא השם שברא ע"י מעשיו
sources.says: Malbim says a name is God's own name, while a remembrance is the name made through His deeds.

sources.quote: זכרו. שמו כי בשם יזכר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says זכרו means His name, since one is remembered by name.

12:7.headline: 'You will return to God', or 'you will rest in God'
12:7.body: תשוב usually means return or repent. Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as 'you will rest', as in 'in quiet and rest you will be saved', and Radak also gives the reading 'return to your God'.

sources.quote: ענין ההשקט ומרגוע כמו בשובה ונחת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means quiet and rest.

sources.quote: ויהיה תשוב ענין תשובה
sources.says: Radak says it can also mean repentance, reading 'in your God' as 'to your God'.

sources.quote: באלהיך תשוב כלומר תנוח כמו בשובה ונחת תושעון
sources.says: Radak first reads it as 'you will rest in your God'.

12:9.headline: Ephraim boasts 'I found און': strength, wealth, or a deed
12:9.body: Radak reads און as strength or as wealth, like הון. A teaching in Rashi reads it as a legal deed, Jeroboam's claim that all Israel were his slaves, and Ibn Ezra hears an echo of Jacob's און, his strength, in verse 4.

sources.quote: און. כמו הון או פירושו כמו כח
sources.says: Radak says און means wealth, or strength.

sources.quote: מָצָאתִי לִי שְׁטַר חוֹב שֶׁיֵּשׁ לִי מַלְכוּת עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says it means strength, and brings a teaching that it is a deed giving Ephraim's king rule over Israel.

sources.quote: והנה אפרים חושב, כי אפרים הוא מצא האון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God gave Jacob his strength, yet Ephraim thinks he found the און himself.

12:10.headline: Back to tents: a promise of Torah study, or a threat?
12:10.body: Rashi reads 'I will make you dwell in tents' as a promise of students of Torah, like Jacob 'who dwelt in tents'. Malbim reads it as a warning: cheat, and you will be poor tent dwellers again, as you were leaving Egypt.

sources.quote: אַעֲמִיד מִתּוֹכְךָ תַּלְמִידִים עוֹסְקִים בַּתּוֹרָה
sources.says: Rashi says God will raise up students busy with Torah in place of the cheating traders.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיָה יַעֲקֹב אִישׁ תָּם יוֹשֵׁב אֹהָלִים
sources.says: Rashi links it to Jacob, 'a simple man who dwelt in tents'.

sources.quote: תשובו להיות עניים יושבי אהלים מחסרון בית ומעון
sources.says: Malbim says it is a threat that they will become poor again, living in tents for lack of a home.

12:15.headline: תמרורים: bitter anger, or stone markers like altars
12:15.body: Radak gives two readings. תמרורים may be heaps of stones, the altars Ephraim built, as in 'set up markers' in Jeremiah 31:21, or it may come from מר, 'bitter', a bitter anger.

sources.quote: והם המזבחות שהיו כגלים וציונים וכמוהו שימי לך תמרורים ויש לפרשו ג"כ מענין מרורים
sources.says: Radak says it means the altars that were like heaps and markers, or else bitterness.

sources.quote: תמרורים. מלשון מר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from bitter.

13:1.headline: A word for trembling found elsewhere only in Aramaic
13:1.body: רתת appears only here. Ibn Ezra says it has no partner word in Hebrew, only in Aramaic, and Malbim says it is Aramaic for fear. Rashi says Jeroboam of Ephraim spoke with trembling. Radak says that when Ephraim spoke, his hearers trembled.

sources.quote: ואין למלת רתת חבר רק בארמית
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word רתת has no partner except in Aramaic.

sources.quote: רתת. חרדה ופחד בלשון ארמי
sources.says: Malbim says רתת is the Aramaic word for trembling and fear.

sources.quote: וְדִבֵּר כְּנֶגֶד שְׁלֹמֹה דְּבָרִים קָשִׁים וּבִרְעָדָה
sources.says: Rashi says Jeroboam spoke harsh words against Solomon, and with trembling.

sources.quote: כי בדברו היה אוחז רתת ורעדה השומע אותו
sources.says: Radak says that when Ephraim spoke, trembling seized whoever heard him.

13:2.headline: Idols made 'in their likeness' or 'by their own cleverness'
13:2.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read כתבונם as 'in their likeness', a short form of תבנית. Radak reads it from תבונה, understanding: they thought about what shape to make and chose a calf. Malbim says the people now made idols by their own understanding.

sources.quote: כִּתְבוּנָם. כְּתַבְנִיתָם
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'like their pattern'.

sources.quote: כמו כתבניתם והוא ענין דמות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is like תבנית and means a likeness.

sources.quote: ופי' כתבונם כמו שהתבוננו בדבר איזו צורה יעשו והסכימו לעשות עגל
sources.says: Radak says it means they considered what shape to make, and agreed on a calf.

sources.quote: ועתה יעשו להם כתבונם לפי הבנתם
sources.says: Malbim says now they make idols according to their own understanding.

13:2.headline: Who sacrifices whom? Three readings of a dark phrase
13:2.body: The verse says זבחי אדם עגלים ישקון. Rashi, following the sages, reads it as the idol priests saying: whoever sacrifices his son may kiss the calf. Radak reads it as people who come to sacrifice. Ibn Ezra says they kiss calves and kill people, the reverse of how people should act.

sources.quote: מִי שֶׁזּוֹבֵחַ בְּנוֹ לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, כְּדַאי הוּא לִהְיוֹת נוֹשֵׁק הָעֵגֶל
sources.says: Rashi says the priests told people that whoever sacrifices his son to the idol is worthy to kiss the calf.

sources.quote: בעבורם הם אומרים כהני העגל לבני אדם הבאים לזבוח
sources.says: Radak says the calf's priests speak to people who come to sacrifice.

sources.quote: והנם הפך כל אדם, כי האדם ישק לאדם שהוא חבירו ויזבח העגלים למאכלו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are the reverse of everyone else, who kiss their fellow men and slaughter calves for food.

13:5.headline: A land of thirst, named with a word found nowhere else
13:5.body: תלאבות appears only here. Rashi says it has no match, and reads it as a mound (תל) where you long (אוב) for every good thing and find none. Ibn Ezra and Radak say it means a land of thirst, and Radak's father proved this from Arabic. Malbim derives it from אבה, to want.

sources.quote: אֵין לוֹ דִּמְיוֹן, וּפִתְרוֹנוֹ לְפִי עִנְיָנוֹ: תֵּל שֶׁאוֹבִין בּוֹ כָּל טוֹבָה וְאֵין מוֹצְאִין
sources.says: Rashi says it has no parallel, and by context it is a mound where people long for every good thing and find nothing.

sources.quote: ארץ ציה וצמא וככה בלשון ישמעאל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means a dry and thirsty land, and the Arabic word means the same.

sources.quote: בארץ צמאה והיא המדבר והביא אדוני אבי ז"ל ראיה למלה הזאת מלשון ערבי
sources.says: Radak says it is a thirsty land, the desert, and his father proved the word from Arabic.

sources.quote: ארץ תאבה וצמאה, ושרשו אבה
sources.says: Malbim says it is a land that longs and thirsts, from the root אבה.

13:7.headline: Not Assyria: 'I will lie in wait'
13:7.body: אשור usually names Assyria. Rashi says this one is written without a dagesh, so it is a verb: I will lie in wait and watch, as in Numbers 24:17. Metzudat Zion and Malbim also read it as watching. The Targum says the leopard lurks on the path.

sources.quote: כָּל ׳אַשּׁוּר׳ שֶׁבַּמִּקְרָא דָּגֵשׁ, וְזֶה רָפֵי, שֶׁאֵינוֹ שֵׁם מָקוֹם אֶלָּא אֶאֱרוֹב וְאֶשְׁקוֹד
sources.says: Rashi says every Ashur in Scripture has a dagesh but this one does not, because it is not a place name but means 'I will lie in wait and watch'.

sources.quote: ענין הבטה וראיה כמו אשורנו ולא קרוב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means looking and seeing, as in Numbers 24:17.

sources.quote: שרשו שור שהיא הבטה מרחוק
sources.says: Malbim says its root is שור, looking from far off.

sources.quote: כְּנִמְרָא כָּמָן עַל שְׁבִילָא
sources.says: The Targum says 'like a leopard lurking on the path'.

13:8.headline: A bear robbed of its cubs, or a bear that robs
13:8.body: Metzudat Zion and Radak say a שכול bear is one whose cubs were killed, so it attacks anyone. Rashi reads the word as active, like חנון: a bear ready to make people lose their children. Ibn Ezra gives both readings.

sources.quote: מי שבניו מתים קרוי שכול
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says one whose children have died is called שכול.

sources.quote: שהרגו בניו והוא שכול ומר נפש
sources.says: Radak says its cubs were killed and it is bereaved and bitter.

sources.quote: כֻּלּוֹ לָבוּשׁ שִׁכּוּלִים וּמוּכָן לְשַׁכֵּל אֲנָשִׁים
sources.says: Rashi says it is wrapped in bereavement and ready to bereave people.

sources.quote: יש אומרים: שנהרגו בניו, או הוא תואר יוצא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some explain that its young were killed, or else it is an active description.

13:8.headline: The bear tears open the chest, or the closed heart
13:8.body: סגור לבם is the closed covering of their heart. Rashi first says the bear rips the chest open down to the heart. His second reading, like Radak's, is their heart that is closed and will not understand.

sources.quote: כְּדֶרֶךְ הַדֹּב אוֹחֵז צִפָּרְנָיו בֶּחָזֶה וְקוֹרֵעַ עַד הַלֵּב
sources.says: Rashi says it is like a bear that sinks its claws into the chest and tears down to the heart.

sources.quote: אֶת לִבָּם הַסָּגוּר מִלְּהָבִין לָשׁוּב אֵלַי
sources.says: Rashi's second reading is their heart, closed against understanding that they should return to God.

sources.quote: לבם שהוא סגור ולא יבין אקרענו
sources.says: Radak says God will tear their heart, which is closed and does not understand.

13:9.headline: 'It ruined you, Israel' answers 'Happy are you, Israel'
13:9.body: Rashi says Israel ruined itself by rebelling against the One who helped it. Malbim hears an answer to Moses' blessing, 'Happy are you, Israel... the shield of your help' (Deuteronomy 33:29). Where Moses said אשריך, happy are you, Hosea says שחתך, it ruined you. Radak says it was the calf that ruined them.

sources.quote: נגד מ"ש אשריך ישראל מי כמוך עם נושע בה' מגן עזרך
sources.says: Malbim says the verse answers 'Happy are you, Israel... saved by the LORD, the shield of your help'.

sources.quote: אינו אשריך רק שחתך
sources.says: Malbim says it is no longer 'happy are you' but 'it ruined you'.

sources.quote: חִבַּלְתָּ עַצְמְךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי בִי פָּשַׁעְתָּ
sources.says: Rashi says Israel ruined itself, because it rebelled against God.

sources.quote: העגל שזכר למעלה אמר הוא שחתך
sources.says: Radak says the calf mentioned earlier is what ruined you.

13:10.headline: 'I will be' or 'Where is'? A word read two ways
13:10.body: The Targum reads אהי as איה, 'where': where is your king now? Ibn Ezra and Radak report this. Rashi says there is no need to change the plain sense: אהי means 'I will be', and God will stand by and watch for your king. The same word comes twice more in verse 14.

sources.quote: אָן מַלְכֵּךְ כְּעַן
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'where is your king now'.

sources.quote: יוֹנָתָן תִּרְגֵּם: ״אַיֵּה מַלְכָּךְ״. וַאֲנִי אוֹמֵר, אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ לְעָקְרוֹ מִמַּשְׁמָעוּתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum reads 'where is your king', but there is no need to take the word from its plain meaning.

sources.quote: יש אומרים: הפוך כמו איה. והנכון: כאומרו: אהי מלכך איפוא הוא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some read it as איה with letters swapped, but the right reading is 'I will be'.

sources.quote: אני אהיה קיים לעולם אבל מלכך איפא
sources.says: Radak says it means 'I will endure forever, but where is your king'.

13:12.headline: Ephraim's sin is tied up in a bundle, kept for later
13:12.body: צרור is something tied up in a bundle, like the money in Genesis 42:35. Rashi and Radak say God keeps Ephraim's sin stored away, not forgotten. Malbim says it is Ephraim who keeps his sins bundled up and will not let them go.

sources.quote: ענין קשירה כמו צרור כספו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means tying up, as in 'his bundle of money' (Genesis 42:35).

sources.quote: שמור הוא אצלי כמו הדבר השמור בתוך הצרור
sources.says: Radak says the sin is kept with God, like something kept inside a bundle.

sources.quote: צָרוּר עֲוֺן אֶפְרָיִם. לֹא וִתַּרְתִּי עָלָיו
sources.says: Rashi says God did not let Ephraim's sin go.

sources.quote: אפרים אינו עוזב את עונותיו רק עונו צרור אצלו
sources.says: Malbim says Ephraim does not leave his sins but keeps them bundled with him.

13:13.headline: A baby too foolish to come out when its time comes
13:13.body: Ephraim is a child who stays at the משבר when it should be born. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say the משבר is the birthing stool. Radak says it is the womb, named for the breaking pains of labor. Radak adds that a wise child would come out at once.

sources.quote: שֶׁהַיּוֹלֶדֶת יוֹשֶׁבֶת עָלָיו לֵילֵד
sources.says: Rashi says it is what a woman in labor sits on to give birth.

sources.quote: הוא מקום מושב היולדת כשכורעת ללדת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the seat of a woman when she kneels to give birth.

sources.quote: ונקרא הרחם משבר מפני חבלי היולדה ושבריה
sources.says: Radak says the womb is called משבר because of the pains and breaking of labor.

sources.quote: כי אם היה חכם לא היה עומד עת אחת במשבר
sources.says: Radak says that if the child were wise, it would not stay at the opening even a moment.

13:15.headline: Among brothers, or among the reeds by the water?
13:15.body: Radak reads בין אחים as 'among his brothers': Ephraim grew greater than the other tribes. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read אחים from אחו, reed grass that grows by water, which the east wind will dry up. Malbim says the prophet plays on both words.

sources.quote: היה הולך וגדל ופורה בין אחיו
sources.says: Radak says Ephraim kept growing and bearing fruit among his brothers.

sources.quote: וַאֲנִי אוֹמֵר ׳אַחִים׳ לְשׁוֹן ״וַתִּרְעֶינָה בָאָחוּ״
sources.says: Rashi says אחים comes from אחו, the reed meadow of Genesis 41:2.

sources.quote: כי הוא בין אחים - מגזרת באחו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אחים comes from the word אחו, reed grass.

sources.quote: ובשם אחים ימתיק שיתוף מלת אחו
sources.says: Malbim says the word אחים sweetly carries a share of the word אחו.

2:2.headline: Jezreel means 'God sows': a scattered people gathered like seed
2:2.body: יזרעאל is a valley's name, but it is also built from זרע, sow, and אל, God. The commentators read 'the day of Jezreel' as the day God gathers Israel, whom He scattered like seed.

sources.quote: יזרעאל. היא מלה מורכבת מן זריעה ומן אל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the name is built from two words: sowing, and God.

sources.quote: ואדוני אבי ז"ל פירש זמן ארוך וגדול היו זרועים בגוים ועתה אקבצם לפיכך קרא שם ישראל יזרעאל שהאל זרעם בגוים
sources.says: Radak brings his father's reading: Israel is called Jezreel because God sowed them among the nations and will now gather them.

sources.quote: יום קבוץ ישראל אשר הפיצם האל כמפזר זרעי׳ ע״פ השדה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is the day Israel is gathered, after God scattered them like seed over a field.

2:4.headline: A doubled word for adultery: unfaithful again and again
2:4.body: The usual word is ניאוף. Here the last letters repeat, נאפופים, and Malbim says the doubling shows the act repeated and kept up.

sources.quote: ונאפוף מורה התמדת הניאוף, שהשמות שנכפל בם למ"ד הפעל מורה על חזוק הפעולה והתמדתה
sources.says: Malbim says the doubled letters in נאפופים show adultery that is strong and constant.

sources.quote: ונאפופיה - כפול הלמ"ד כמו סגריר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra notes that the last root letter is doubled, as in סגריר.

2:7.headline: The mother who conceived them, or their teachers?
2:7.body: הורתם can come from הריון, pregnancy: 'she who conceived them acted shamefully'. Targum Jonathan and Rashi read it from הוראה, teaching: 'their teachers were put to shame'.

sources.quote: בְּהִיתוּ מַלְפֵיהוֹן (תרגום יונתן) הַחֲכָמִים הַמּוֹרִים לָהֶם הוֹרָאוֹת, בּוֹשִׁים מִפְּנֵי עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ
sources.says: Rashi, following Targum Jonathan, reads it as 'their teachers': the sages who instruct them are shamed before the common people.

sources.quote: הורתם. מלשון הריון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from הריון, pregnancy: the mother who conceived them.

sources.quote: ופה הוסיף שהובישה אותו גם מצד ההריון
sources.says: Malbim says she shamed her children even in how they were conceived.

2:11.headline: Usually 'I will rescue'; here 'I will take away'
2:11.body: והצלתי normally means 'I will save'. Here God takes back the wool and linen He gave, and Rashi says every הצלה in Scripture really means lifting something off and setting it apart.

sources.quote: כָּל ׳הַצָּלָה׳ שֶׁבַּמִּקְרָא לְשׁוֹן תְּרוּמָה וְהַפְרָשָׁה הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says every הצלה in Scripture means lifting off and separating, as in Genesis 31:9.

sources.quote: והצלתי - והפרשתי וכן כל לשון הצלה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means 'I will separate', and so does every use of הצלה.

sources.quote: וענין והצלתי כענין אשר הציל אלהים מאבינו ענין ההסרה והשלילה
sources.says: Radak says it means removing and taking away, as when God 'took' Laban's wealth in Genesis.

2:15.headline: A jewelry word that Rashi explains from Arabic
2:15.body: חליה is a piece of jewelry. Rashi explains it from the Arabic word for ornament, and Malbim says it was a hollow ring worn around the ear.

sources.quote: וְחֶלְיָתָהּ. בִּלְשׁוֹן עַרְבִי הוּא קִשּׁוּט
sources.says: Rashi says that in Arabic this word means an ornament.

sources.quote: וּבִלְשׁוֹן עֲרָבִי אַלְחַלוּ
sources.says: Rashi says a set of women's jewelry is called אלחלו in Arabic, and ties it to this verse.

sources.quote: הנזם תולה בנקב שבתנוך האזן, והחלי חלול ועגול ומקיף את האזן
sources.says: Malbim, citing this verse, says the נזם hangs from the ear lobe and the חלי is a hollow ring around the ear.

2:17.headline: Her vineyards, or her leaders?
2:17.body: Read plainly, God gives back the vineyards He ruined in verse 14. Targum Jonathan, quoted by Rashi, reads כרמיה as 'her leaders', the people who provide for her.

sources.quote: תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן לְשׁוֹן פַּרְנָסִים וּמַנְהִיגִים
sources.says: Rashi says Targum Jonathan reads it as 'providers and leaders'.

sources.quote: וַאֲמַנֵי לָהּ יַת פַּרְנָסָהָא מִתַּמָן
sources.says: Targum Jonathan translates 'I will appoint her leaders from there'.

sources.quote: ומה שזכר כרמיה לפי שזכר בפורענות והשימותי גפנה אמר בנחמה כרמיה
sources.says: Radak reads real vineyards, named because verse 14 threatened to ruin her vines.

2:17.headline: The Valley of Trouble becomes a doorway of hope
2:17.body: Achor, from עכר, 'trouble', is the valley where Achan was punished in Joshua's time. Radak says its shameful name will be replaced by a good one: Door of Hope.

sources.quote: מליצה נלקחת משם המקום שעשו שם שפטים בעכן שעבר על החרם והיה לו לפתח תקוה
sources.says: Malbim says the phrase comes from the place where Achan was judged for taking banned spoil, and it became for him an opening of hope.

sources.quote: ואותו עמק עכור לא יקרא עוד כן כי שמו הוא לגנאי אלא יקרא לו שם לשבח והוא פתח תקוה
sources.says: Radak says the valley's name is a shameful one, and it will be called by a name of praise, Door of Hope.

sources.quote: עכור. ענין השחתה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says עכור means ruin.

2:17.headline: She will sing there, or she will live there?
2:17.body: וענתה can mean 'she will sing', like Miriam at the sea. Rashi reads it as 'she will dwell there', from מעון, a dwelling.

sources.quote: וענתה. ענינו הרמת קול שירה כמו ותען להם מרים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means raising the voice in song, like Miriam's song.

sources.quote: וְעָנְתָה שָׁמָּה. לְשׁוֹן ׳דִּירָה׳
sources.says: Rashi says it means dwelling, like מעון, a den.

sources.quote: וענתה - תנגן ותשיר, כמו: ותען להם מרים. ויש אומרים: ותדור שמה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads 'she will sing', and mentions others who read 'she will dwell', which he finds far-fetched.

2:18.headline: 'My husband', not 'my master': a word that sounds like an idol
2:18.body: Both אישי and בעלי can mean 'my husband'. Rashi says בעלי sounds like a master to be feared, and Metzudat David adds that בעל is also the name of the idol Baal.

sources.quote: בַּעְלִי. לְשׁוֹן אַדְנוּת וּמוֹרָא
sources.says: Rashi says בעלי speaks of mastery and fear, while אישי speaks of marriage and young love.

sources.quote: לפי ששם הבעל הוא משותף לשם עבודת גלולים
sources.says: Metzudat David says the word בעל is shared with the name of an idol, so she will not say it.

sources.quote: לכן בעבור היות שם בעל ספק עם הבעל, שהוא צלם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that because בעל can be confused with Baal, an idol, she must not use even a word that could sound like it.

2:22.headline: Betrothed 'in faith': whose faith, and what kind?
2:22.body: באמונה can mean 'in faithfulness', 'as a reward for your trust', or 'firmly, for good'. Ibn Ezra, Rashi and Radak each take a different one.

sources.quote: וארשתיך לי באמונה. שענינו בקיום שלא ימוט לעולם
sources.says: Radak says אמונה here means lasting firmness: a bond that will never give way.

sources.quote: בִּשְׂכַר הָאֱמוּנָה שֶׁהֶאֱמַנְתְּ בַּגּוֹלָה
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'as a reward for the faith you kept in exile'.

sources.quote: תהיי לי לבדי באמונה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means faithfulness: you will be mine alone.

2:23.headline: God 'answers' the sky: a chain of requests from seed to heaven
2:23.body: אענה usually means 'I will answer'. Metzudat David and Malbim picture the land asking the sky for rain and the sky asking God; Ibn Ezra reads it simply as 'I will provide'.

sources.quote: כי בהעצר השמים כאלו ישאלו להוריד המטר ואמר שישיב על שאלתם
sources.says: Metzudat David says that when rain is held back the skies are pictured as asking for it, and God answers them.

sources.quote: מצייר במליצתו שהזרע הנזרעת בארץ היא שואלת ודורשת מן הדגן והתירוש
sources.says: Malbim pictures a chain of requests: the seed asks the grain, the grain asks the earth, the earth asks the sky, and the sky asks God.

sources.quote: כמו: והכסף יענה את הכל - ימציא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means 'provide', as in 'money answers everything'.

2:25.headline: 'I will sow her': Jezreel turns from scattering to planting
2:25.body: The verse plays on יזרעאל, 'God sows', from the verse before. Radak says the same name first meant Israel scattered among the nations, and now means Israel planted in its own land.

sources.quote: בפורענות קרא שם ישראל יזרעאל לפי שהיו זרועים בגוים ובזמן הישועה קורא אותם ג"כ יזרעאל שהיו נזרעים בארצם, לפיכך אמר אחריו וזרעתיה לי בארץ
sources.says: Radak says that in punishment Israel was called Jezreel because it was sown among the nations, and in redemption because it is sown in its own land, so the next verse says 'I will sow her'.

sources.quote: כְּזוֹרֵעַ סְאָה לְהַכְנִיס כַּמָּה כּוֹרִין, כֵּן יִתְוַסְּפוּ עֲלֵיהֶן בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל כַּמָּה גֵּרִים
sources.says: Rashi, from the Talmud, says it is like sowing a small measure of seed to reap many times more: many converts will join them.

4:2.headline: 'Blood touches blood': so many killings, or sin piled on sin?
4:2.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it plainly: there were so many killings that one victim's blood ran into the next. Targum Jonathan reads דָּמִים as sins: 'they add sins on top of sins'.

sources.quote: עַד נָגַע דַּם הָרוּג זֶה בְּדַם חֲבֵרוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the plain sense is so much bloodshed that one victim's blood touched another's.

sources.quote: דמי הרוג אחד נוגעים בדמי הרוג אחר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the blood of one slain man touches the blood of another.

sources.quote: וְחוֹבִין עַל חוֹבִין מוֹסְפִּין
sources.says: Targum Jonathan translates: and they add sins upon sins.

4:3.headline: Even the fish will die: worse than the Flood?
4:3.body: In Noah's flood the fish survived. Ibn Ezra reports Yefet's view that this generation was worse than the Flood's, but calls it a sermon; Radak says it is an overstatement, or a curse on the sea near the land of Israel.

sources.quote: ויפת אמר: כי אלה רעים מדור המבול כי דגי הים לא מתו. וזה דרך דרש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Yefet held these people were worse than the generation of the Flood, when the fish did not die, and calls this a sermon.

sources.quote: אֲבָל דָּגִים שֶׁבַּיָּם לֹא מֵתוּ
sources.says: Radak says the fish in the sea did not die in the Flood.

sources.quote: שָׁם נֶאֱמַר דֶּרֶךְ גּוּזְמָא
sources.says: Radak says the verse in Hosea is said as an overstatement.

sources.quote: וזה בים ארץ ישראל שהיתה בארץ קללת האל יתברך בעון יושביה ביבשה ובים
sources.says: Radak says it means the sea of the land of Israel, cursed on land and at sea for its people's sin.

4:5.headline: 'I will cut off your mother', or 'your mother became like you'?
4:5.body: Radak and the Metzudat Zion read וְדָמִיתִי as 'I will cut off', and 'your mother' as the whole community of Israel. Malbim reads it from דִּמְיוֹן, likeness: the nation, the mother, answers the priest, 'I have become like you'.

sources.quote: וכרתי כניסתך, כלומר שלא תשאר בישראל כנסיה
sources.says: Radak says it means I will cut off your community, so that no community is left in Israel.

sources.quote: ענין כריתה כמו ער מואב נדמה
sources.says: The Metzudat Zion says the word means cutting off.

sources.quote: אמך. הכנסייא
sources.says: The Metzudat Zion says 'your mother' is the community.

sources.quote: דמיתי אמך א"כ אני דומה לך אני אמך
sources.says: Malbim reads it as the nation saying: I, your mother, have become like you.

4:6.headline: 'My people נדמו': destroyed, gone foolish, or grown like you?
4:6.body: Radak says נִדְמוּ means cut off, while Targum Jonathan translates 'my people have become foolish'. Malbim says they became like the priest who rejected knowledge, but Ibn Ezra objects that this sense would need the word אֶל after it.

sources.quote: נדמו עמי. גם זה ענין כריתה
sources.says: Radak says this too means being cut off.

sources.quote: אִטַפַּשׁוּ עַמִי מִבְּלִי דַעְתָּא
sources.says: Targum Jonathan translates: my people became foolish for lack of knowledge.

sources.quote: נדמו. מענין דמוין, ר"ל נדמו אליך
sources.says: Malbim says it comes from likeness: they became like you.

sources.quote: זאת המלה אם היתה מגזרת דמות יהיה אחריה אל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that if the word came from 'likeness', it would be followed by the word אל.

4:8.headline: The priests 'eat the sin' of the people: the sin-offering
4:8.body: חַטָּאת is both a sin and the offering brought for it. Radak and the Metzudat David say the priests cared only for eating the people's sin-offerings, and so they hoped the people would sin.

sources.quote: ורק אוחזים בכהונה לאכול בשר חטאת עמי
sources.says: The Metzudat David says they hold the priesthood only to eat the meat of the people's sin-offerings.

sources.quote: אומרים מתי יחטאו ויביאו חטאת ואשם ונאכלם
sources.says: Radak says the priests ask: when will they sin and bring sin-offerings and guilt-offerings for us to eat?

sources.quote: נַעֲשׂוּ לָהֶם כֹּהֲנֵי בָּמוֹת וְאוֹכְלִין מַה שֶּׁהָיוּ כֹּהֲנִים רְאוּיִין לֶאֱכוֹל
sources.says: Rashi says the false prophets became priests of the shrines and ate what true priests should have eaten.

4:12.headline: 'His staff tells him': a diviner's stick, or a beating?
4:12.body: Rashi, from the midrash, says this is a diviner who holds his staff and asks it, 'Shall I go or not?' Radak's father said the people are like a blind man led by his cane, the false prophets; Malbim says the only answer they will get is the stick that beats them.

sources.quote: הָאוֹחֵז אֶת מַקְלוֹ וְאוֹמֵר אִם אֵלֵךְ אִם לֹא אֵלֵךְ
sources.says: Rashi says a diviner is one who holds his staff and says 'Shall I go or not go?', and cites this verse.

sources.quote: הם כמו העור שיורה לו מקלו הדרך שהוא הולך בה, ומקלו הם נביאי השקר
sources.says: Radak says they are like a blind man whose cane shows him the way, and the cane is the false prophets.

sources.quote: רק עץ אחר יגיד להם התשובה שהוא המקל המוכן להכות אותם
sources.says: Malbim says another piece of wood will give them the answer: the stick ready to beat them.

4:14.headline: Yeparedu: they go apart, they band together, or act like mules?
4:14.body: Radak says the men leave their wives to go off with prostitutes. Targum Jonathan, as Rashi explains it, says they band together to drink, and Radak's father heard פֶּרֶד, a mule, in the word.

sources.quote: כי הם יפרידו עצמם מנשיהם
sources.says: Radak says they separate themselves from their wives.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן ׳סִיעָה׳, כְּלוֹמַר מִתְחַבְּרִין אַתֶּם לִשְׁתּוֹת יַיִן
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum reads it as a band of people: you join together to drink wine.

sources.quote: ואדוני אבי ז"ל כתבו מענין פרד ר"ל כי הם שטופים בזמה כמו הפרד
sources.says: Radak says his father took it from the word for mule, since they are as given to lust as a mule.

4:14.headline: The prophet calls the shrine prostitutes 'holy women'
4:14.body: The Metzudat Zion says the קְדֵשׁוֹת are prostitutes. Malbim says idol worshippers set such women apart for their god and thought it holy, so the name is given to them in scorn.

sources.quote: הקדשות. הזונות כמו לא תהיה קדשה
sources.says: The Metzudat Zion says the קדשות are prostitutes.

sources.quote: ועובדי ע"ז היו להם קדשות מיוחדות לזנות לשם פסל הזימה
sources.says: Malbim says idol worshippers had women set aside for this in the name of their idol.

sources.quote: ולגנאי הונח עליהן שם קדשה, הפך מה שהיה בזה קדושה לפי דעתם
sources.says: Malbim says the name קדשה was given to them in scorn, against their own belief that it was holy.

4:15.headline: Beth-el, 'House of God', renamed Beth-aven, 'House of Wickedness'
4:15.body: Jacob named the place Beth-el because God appeared to him there. Radak says that after Jeroboam set up a golden calf there, the prophets called it Beth-aven in scorn, because the calf was empty and wicked.

sources.quote: כי יעקב אבינו קרא למקום בית אל מפני המראה שראה בו ונגלה שם האל
sources.says: Radak says Jacob called the place Beth-el because of the vision he saw there, when God appeared to him.

sources.quote: כינו הנביאים שמו וקראו אותו בית און כי העגל שוא ואון היה
sources.says: Radak says the prophets renamed it Beth-aven, because the calf was falsehood and wickedness.

sources.quote: וגם זה הוא לשון נופל על הלשון כי בית אל כינה הכתוב לגנאי בשם בית און
sources.says: The Metzudat David calls it a play on words: the Bible calls Beth-el by the scornful name Beth-aven.

4:16.headline: Grazing 'in a wide place': a punishment or a gift?
4:16.body: Rashi says God will now feed Israel sparingly, like a lamb that must roam an open field for grass. Malbim objects that a wide pasture means plenty, and Radak says God would have fed them richly had they not rebelled.

sources.quote: עַתָּה יִרְעֵם מִרְעִית מְצֻמְצֶמֶת כְּכֶבֶשׂ הָרוֹעֶה בַּמֶּרְחָב
sources.says: Rashi says God will now feed them a scant diet, like a lamb grazing in the open.

sources.quote: פירש"י מרעית מצומצמת, והלשון משמע בהפך
sources.says: Malbim says Rashi explains it as scant grazing, but the words mean the opposite.

sources.quote: לולי שסרר היה רועה אותם ה' בשפע כמו הכבשים במרחב
sources.says: Radak says that had Israel not rebelled, God would have fed them in plenty, like sheep in a wide pasture.

4:19.headline: 'The wind has bound her in its wings': exile, or empty hands?
4:19.body: Rashi says Israel is like a bird the wind will not let land, carrying it far away into exile. Radak says it is like a man who ties up wind in the corner of his robe and opens it to find nothing, as Israel found nothing in its idols.

sources.quote: כַּעוֹף הַזֶּה שֶׁאֵין הָרוּחַ מַנִּיחָתוֹ לִשְׁכּוֹן עַד שֶׁמּוֹלִיכוֹ לְמֵרָחוֹק
sources.says: Rashi says it is like a bird the wind does not let settle until it carries it far away.

sources.quote: כמו האדם שיצרור הרוח בכנפיו וכשיתיר כנפיו לא ימצא כלום
sources.says: Radak says it is like a man who ties wind in the corner of his garment and finds nothing when he unties it.

sources.quote: כְּמָא דְלֵית אֶפְשַׁר לְמֵיצַר רוּחַ בְּכָנָף
sources.says: Targum Jonathan says it is as impossible as tying up wind in a corner of cloth.

5:2.headline: "They went deeper than I did": a rule turned upside down
5:2.body: Rashi reads "they went deep" against God's own law. God said whoever does not go up to the Temple breaks a command, and they decreed that whoever goes up is killed.

sources.quote: אֲנִי אָמַרְתִּי כָּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ עוֹלֶה לָרֶגֶל עוֹבֵר בַּעֲשֵׂה, וְהֵם גָּזְרוּ כָּל הָעוֹלֶה לָרֶגֶל יֵהָרֵג, הֲרֵי שֶׁהֶעְמִיקוּ יוֹתֵר מִמֶּנִּי
sources.says: Rashi has God say: I said whoever does not go up for the festival breaks a command, and they decreed whoever goes up is killed, so they went deeper than I did.

5:2.headline: "And I am rebuke": the prophet calls himself a man of warning
5:2.body: The verse reads "and I am rebuke to them all". Radak and Malbim say the word "man" is left out, as in "and I am prayer", so it means "I am a man of rebuke".

sources.quote: ואני מוסר. חסר איש כמו ואני תפלה שפירושו ואני איש תפילה
sources.says: Radak says the word "man" is missing, as in "and I am prayer", which means "I am a man of prayer".

sources.quote: ואני מוסר. אני איש מוסר, כמו ואני תפלה, איש תפלה
sources.says: Malbim says it means "I am a man of rebuke", like "I am prayer" means a man of prayer.

sources.quote: כי אני איש מוסר לכלם ויום ויום אני מייסר אותם ולא ישמעו לי
sources.says: Radak has the prophet say he rebukes them every day and they do not listen.

5:6.headline: God "slipped away" from them, like a garment pulled off
5:6.body: They come with sheep and cattle to seek God and do not find Him. Rashi says חלץ means slipped off, the way clothes are stripped off a person.

sources.quote: נִשְׁמַט, כְּמוֹ (שמואל ב ב:כא) ״וְקַח לְךָ אֶת חֲלִצָתוֹ״ – בְּגָדִים שֶׁתַּשְׁמִיט מֵעֲלֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it means slipped away, like "take his armor", the clothes you strip off someone.

sources.quote: חלץ. נפרד מהם וסר מעליהם
sources.says: Radak says it means He separated from them and left them.

5:8.headline: Gibeah and Ramah: the Targum hears Saul and Samuel
5:8.body: Hosea names two towns in Benjamin. Targum Jonathan, quoted by Rashi, hears in them Saul of Gibeah, whom the people made king, and Samuel of Ramah, whom they did not heed.

sources.quote: עַל דְאַמְלִיכוּ יַת שְׁאוּל דְמִגִבְעֲתָא
sources.says: The Targum says the trumpet blows "because they made Saul of Gibeah king".

sources.quote: בְּעָוֹן שֶׁהִמְלִיכוּ עֲלֵיהֶם אֶת שָׁאוּל שֶׁהָיָה בַּגִּבְעָה (שמואל א י:כו), וְלֹא שָׁמְעוּ לְקוֹל שְׁמוּאֵל שֶׁהָיָה מִן הָרָמָה
sources.says: Rashi quotes Jonathan: the sword comes for the sin of crowning Saul, who was from Gibeah, and not heeding Samuel, who was from Ramah.

5:8.headline: "After you, Benjamin": the enemy behind, or the delay?
5:8.body: Plainly the enemy is right behind Benjamin. Rashi also hears אחר as "delay": they held back from going up to the Temple, which stood in Benjamin's land.

sources.quote: עַל שֶׁאִחַרְתֶּם וַחֲזַרְתֶּם אָחוֹר מִלַּעֲלוֹת לָרֶגֶל לְבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, שֶׁהוּא בְּחֶלְקוֹ שֶׁל בִּנְיָמִין
sources.says: Rashi says it is because they delayed and turned back from going up to the Temple, which is in Benjamin's portion.

sources.quote: ר״ל כי האויב הולך אחריך להלחם בך
sources.says: Metzudat David says the enemy is coming after you to fight you.

sources.quote: ויזהירו את העם לאמר אחריך בנימין שלא ילכו אחרי מלכות אפרים רק שילכו אחריך אתה בנימין
sources.says: Malbim reads it as a call to follow Benjamin, which was joined to Judah, and not the kingdom of Ephraim.

5:13.headline: A wound named for the medicine sprinkled on it
5:13.body: מזור is a rare word for a wound. Metzudat Zion, Radak and Ibn Ezra say it is named for the healing powder that is sprinkled, זורים, on it.

sources.quote: כן נקרא המכה ע״ש שזורים עליה אבק מסממני׳ המרפאין
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the wound is called this because healing powder is sprinkled on it.

sources.quote: כמו מכתו כי המכה לפי שיזורו אותה נקראת מזור
sources.says: Radak says it means his wound, called מזור because it is sprinkled.

sources.quote: מכה שהיא צריכה שיזורו אותה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a wound that needs to have something sprinkled on it.

5:13.headline: King Yarev: a place, or "the king who will fight for him"?
5:13.body: Ibn Ezra and Radak take ירב as a place name in Assyria. Malbim hears the word ריב, a quarrel: Judah sent to the king so that he would fight its fight.

sources.quote: ירב - שם מקום באשור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Yarev is the name of a place in Assyria.

sources.quote: הוא שם עיר בארץ אשור ובזה הספר זוכר אותו שתי פעמים ואפשר כי אשור היו לו שני שמות
sources.says: Radak says it is a city in Assyria, mentioned twice in this book, or Assyria had two names.

sources.quote: ולא להשתעבד אליו רק שירב ריבו מיד שונאיו, לכן קראו מלך ירב
sources.says: Malbim says Judah sent not to serve him but so he would fight its fight against its enemies, so he is called "king Yarev".

5:15.headline: Until they admit guilt, or until they are laid waste?
5:15.body: Rashi and Radak read יאשמו as owning up to guilt. Ibn Ezra also offers "until they are laid waste", linking the word to שממה, desolation.

sources.quote: יַחֲזִיקוּ עַצְמָם כַּאֲשֵׁמִים לְהוֹדוֹת עַל אַשְׁמָתָם
sources.says: Rashi says it means they will consider themselves guilty and confess their guilt.

sources.quote: שיודו שאשמו, או כטעם שממה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means they will admit their guilt, or it means desolation.

sources.quote: וענינו עד שישימו עצמם אשמים
sources.says: Radak says it means until they count themselves guilty.

7:1.headline: Raiders spread out, or a thief stripping people in the street?
7:1.body: Rashi reads פשט as bands of robbers spreading out to rob. Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion read it as stripping off clothes: a thief who once stole in secret now strips people openly.

sources.quote: וְאַף פּוֹשְׁטִים גְּדוּדֵיהֶם בְּלִסְטִיּוּת לְלַסְטֵם אֶת הַבְּרִיּוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says they even send out their bands of robbers to rob people.

sources.quote: יבוא ויפשוט בגדי גדוד אנשים בחוץ לעין כל ולא יפחוד ממי
sources.says: Metzudat David says the thief strips the clothes off a band of people outside, in front of everyone, and fears no one.

sources.quote: פשט. ענין הסרת המלבוש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says פשט means taking off clothing.

7:3.headline: Lying to each other, or denying God?
7:3.body: כחש means lying. Radak gives two readings: they denied God when they hailed the golden calves, or they lied to one another, and either way it pleased the princes.

sources.quote: שכחשו בה' ואמרו אלה אלהיך ישראל
sources.says: Radak says they denied God and said of the calves, "These are your gods, Israel".

sources.quote: ובכחשיהם שמכחשים ומשקרים איש בעמיתו משמחים השרים
sources.says: Radak also reads it as lying to one another, which pleased the princes.

sources.quote: הכחש יבא גם על הכחשת האמונה
sources.says: Malbim says כחש is also used for denying faith in God.

7:4.headline: Exiled "from the city", or the urge that "stirs them up"?
7:4.body: Targum Jonathan reads מעיר as "from their cities", where they will be exiled. Rashi says he cannot fit that to the words, and reads it as the evil urge that stirs them up.

sources.quote: יוֹנָתָן תִּרְגֵּם מַה שֶׁתִּרְגֵּם, וְאֵינִי יָכוֹל לְיַשֵּׁב בּוֹ לְשׁוֹן הַמִּקְרָא. וּלְפִי מַשְׁמָעוֹ, יִשְׁבּוֹת יִצְרָם הָרָע שֶׁהָיָה מֵעִירָם
sources.says: Rashi says he cannot fit Jonathan's translation to the words, and by the plain sense their evil urge, which was stirring them up, rests.

sources.quote: בְּכֵן יִגְלוּן בִּפְרִיעַ מִקִרְוֵיהוֹן
sources.says: The Targum renders it "then they will be exiled quickly from their cities".

sources.quote: מעיר. מלשון התעוררות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says מעיר means stirring up.

7:5.headline: Who got sick: the princes, or the king they plied with wine?
7:5.body: Rashi reads that the princes became sick from wine. Ibn Ezra and Radak read that the princes made the king sick, pouring him wine on his coronation day.

sources.quote: נַעֲשׂוּ שָׂרֵינוּ חוֹלִים
sources.says: Rashi says our princes became sick.

sources.quote: החלו שרים - את המלך מן השכרות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the princes made the king sick with drunkenness.

sources.quote: עד שהחלו המלך מרוב שתות היין
sources.says: Radak says they made the king sick from too much wine.

7:5.headline: Wineskins, or the heat of wine?
7:5.body: חמת can mean a leather bottle, like the one Hagar filled with water, or heat and venom. Radak pictures each prince bringing his own wineskin, while Rashi reads the heat of the wine burning in them.

sources.quote: חמת. הוא נאד וכן וחמת מים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חמת is a leather bottle, as in "a bottle of water".

sources.quote: שהיה זה בא בנאדו מלא יין וזה בא בנאדו ומשקין המלך
sources.says: Radak says each one came with his bottle full of wine and gave the king to drink.

sources.quote: מֵחוֹם הַיַּיִן הַבּוֹעֵר בָּם
sources.says: Rashi says it is the heat of the wine burning in them.

sources.quote: חמת. לשון חמום או ארס
sources.says: Malbim says חמת means heat or venom.

7:5.headline: Princes before the wine, scoffers after it
7:5.body: לצצים is found only here. Radak quotes his father: the verse calls them princes before they drink and scoffers after, and Rashi brings a midrash in which the king sat two scoffers beside any decent man.

sources.quote: וכתב אדוני אבי ז"ל בתחלה קראם שרים קודם שישכרו ואח"כ קראם לוצצים
sources.says: Radak quotes his father: first it calls them princes, before they got drunk, and afterward it calls them scoffers.

sources.quote: כַּד הֲוָה חָמֵי בַּר נָשׁ כָּשֵׁר, הֲוָה מוֹתִיב גַּבֵּיהּ תְּרֵין לֵיצָנִין
sources.says: Rashi brings a midrash: whenever the king saw a decent man, he sat two scoffers next to him.

sources.quote: וזאת המלה מפועלי הכפל, שהוא לצץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from a doubled root, לצץ.

7:7.headline: They "ate" their judges: they killed the court that protested
7:7.body: Here "ate" means killed. Rashi says they killed their Sanhedrin for protesting, and brings a midrash in which Jeroboam said he feared the Sanhedrin and the people answered, "We will kill them".

sources.quote: הָרְגוּ אֶת סַנְהֶדְרִין שֶׁלָּהֶם, לְפִי שֶׁהָיוּ מוֹחִים בְּיָדָם
sources.says: Rashi says they killed their Sanhedrin because it protested against them.

sources.quote: אָמַר לוֹן, ״אֲנָא דָחִיל מִן סַנְהֶדְרִין דִּילְכוֹן״. אָמְרוּן לֵיהּ, ״אֲנַן קָטְלִינַן לוֹן״
sources.says: Rashi quotes the midrash: Jeroboam said, "I fear your Sanhedrin", and they said, "We will kill them".

sources.quote: ואכלו. ר״ל הרגו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says "ate" means killed.

7:8.headline: Ephraim "mixes itself" into the nations, a word from Babel
7:8.body: יתבולל means to mix oneself in. Radak ties it to Babel, where God mixed up the languages: Ephraim blended into the nations God had set it apart from, and Ibn Ezra says they kept running to one nation for help against another.

sources.quote: כמו כי שם בלל ה' שפת כל הארץ ענין בלבול וערבוב
sources.says: Radak says it is like "there God mixed up the language of all the earth", meaning confusion and mixing.

sources.quote: כמו בלול מעורב. והטעם: שהם מבקשים עזר מן האומות לזה מפני זה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means mixed, because they ask the nations for help, one against the other.

sources.quote: יְבֻלְבַּל בַּגּוֹלָה בֵּין הָאֻמּוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says Ephraim will be mixed up in exile among the nations.

7:8.headline: A cake left unturned: burnt below, raw on top
7:8.body: A flat cake baked on coals has to be flipped. Radak says Ephraim is like one never turned: it never turned its plans over and weighed them, and so it chose the calves.

sources.quote: עֻגָה חַרָרָה שֶׁאוֹפִין עַל הַגֶּחָלִים
sources.says: Rashi says an ugah is a flat cake baked on coals.

sources.quote: אם אין הופכים אותה היא נשרפת מתחת ואינה נאפה מלמעלה כן היא העצה שאיננה נכונה כשאין הופכין אותה מענין לענין
sources.says: Radak says an unturned cake burns below and stays raw on top, and so does a plan that is not turned over from side to side.

sources.quote: ובעבור כי דמה יצרם ולבם לתנור, דמה העצה לעוגה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that since the prophet compared their hearts to an oven, he compared their plans to a cake.

7:11.headline: A silly dove, easily lured into the net
7:11.body: פותה comes from luring, which is why a fool is called פתי. Radak says a dove pecks at grain without seeing the net, and walks along innocently because it has no gall.

sources.quote: פותה. מל׳ פתוי ולכן יקרא הסכל פתי כי הוא נפתה בקל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is from luring, and so a fool is called פתי, because he is easily lured.

sources.quote: אלא יונה לפי שאין לה מרה היא כאלו הולכת בתמימות ולא תרגיש על הרע שימצאנה
sources.says: Radak says the dove is named because it has no gall, so it goes along innocently and does not sense the harm waiting for it.

sources.quote: ופירש בעל הערוך שריחתא מבכה וגורדת פניה
sources.says: Radak adds that the Arukh explains the Targum's word for the dove as one that weeps and scratches its face.

7:12.headline: Punish them, or bind them? Menachem and Dunash disagree
7:12.body: Rashi brings two early grammarians. Menachem read the word as binding, like bonds, and Dunash as punishment, with an extra י.

sources.quote: וּמְנַחֵם פֵּרֵשׁ: לְשׁוֹן ׳קֶשֶׁר׳ וּ״מוֹסְרוֹתֶיךָ אֲנַתֵּק״ (ירמיהו ל:ח). אֲבָל דּוֹנַשׁ פָּתַר: לְשׁוֹן ׳יִסּוּרִין׳
sources.says: Rashi says Menachem explained it as binding, as in "I will tear off your bonds", but Dunash explained it as punishment.

sources.quote: איסירם - כמו איסרם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the same as "I will chastise them".

7:14.headline: Full barns, wandering, or crowding together over grain?
7:14.body: Rashi hears מגורות, granaries: they have full barns, so they rebel. Metzudat Zion reads it as wandering to live abroad, and Radak as crowding together when grain comes to town.

sources.quote: יֵשׁ לָהֶם מְגוּרוֹת שֶׁל דָּגָן, לְפִיכָךְ יָסוּרוּ וְיִמְרְדוּ בִּי
sources.says: Rashi says they have granaries of grain, and so they turn away and rebel against Me.

sources.quote: יתגוררו. מלשון גרות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from living as a stranger.

sources.quote: יתגוררו. ענין אסיפה וחבור
sources.says: Radak says it means gathering and banding together.

7:16.headline: A treacherous bow: aimed north, it shoots south
7:16.body: Rashi says a deceitful bow sends the arrow the wrong way. Malbim says the princes who informed on their king were like a bow whose arrow flies back into the archer's heart.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁרוֹצֶה לִירוֹת בּוֹ חֵץ לַצָּפוֹן הוּא יוֹרֶה לַדָּרוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says when you want to shoot an arrow north with it, it shoots south.

sources.quote: שמי שמורה בו חץ חוזר החץ אל לב המורה
sources.says: Malbim says whoever shoots an arrow from it has the arrow come back into his own heart.

sources.quote: כך ישראל פעמים היו שבים לדרך טובה וברגע היו שבים לדרך רעה
sources.says: Radak says Israel would sometimes turn to the good way and in a moment turn back to the bad.

8:4.headline: They made princes, or they removed kings
8:4.body: השירו is spelled with ש, 'they made princes'. Rashi brings a second reading with ס: 'they removed' one king and crowned another. Rashi and Malbim say the Masorah lists it among words written with ש and read as ס.

sources.quote: הֵשִׂירוּ. עָשׂוּ שָׂרִים. דָּבָר אַחֵר: הֵסִירוּ אֶת זֶה מִמְּלוּכָה וְהִמְלִיכוּ אֶת זֶה
sources.says: Rashi says it means they made princes; or else, they removed one king and crowned another.

sources.quote: שֶׁחִבְּרוֹ בַּמָּסוֹרָה כָּתְבִין שִׁי״ן וְקָרִיָּן סָמֶ״ךְ
sources.says: Rashi says the Masorah groups it with words written with shin and read with samekh.

sources.quote: חד מן מלין דכתיבין שי"ן וקרי סמ"ך ונמסר במסורה
sources.says: Malbim says it is one of the words written with shin and read with samekh, as handed down in the Masorah.

8:5.headline: Who left whom: God, the calf, or Samaria?
8:5.body: זנח means to push away or to go far. Rashi says God rejected Samaria for the calf. Metzudat David says the calf abandoned Samaria in its trouble. Radak adds that the calf itself went far away, broken up by Assyria.

sources.quote: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶתְכֶם בְּנֵי שׁוֹמְרוֹן בַּעֲוֹן עֲגָלִים
sources.says: Rashi says God rejected you, people of Samaria, for the sin of the calves.

sources.quote: הנה העגל שעבדת לו עזב אותך ולא עזר לך
sources.says: Metzudat David says the calf you served abandoned you and did not help you.

sources.quote: או יהיה זנח פעל עומד ופי' רחק
sources.says: Radak says the verb may also mean 'went far'.

sources.quote: כי מלך אשור כשלכד שמרון וערי ישראל שבר את העגלים ולקח הזהב
sources.says: He says that when the king of Assyria took Samaria, he broke the calves and took the gold.

8:6.headline: The calf will become splinters: a word found only here
8:6.body: שבבים appears only here. Rashi and Radak read it as chips, like the Aramaic for a sliver off a beam. Ibn Ezra links it to שביבים, sparks. Malbim reads it as 'wayward': Israel itself will be wild children.

sources.quote: וְלָשׁוֹן אֲרַמִּית הוּא שִׁיבָא מִכְּשׁוּרָא
sources.says: Rashi says it is Aramaic, as in 'a splinter from a beam'.

sources.quote: שבבים. כמו שברים וחתיכות
sources.says: Radak says it means broken bits and pieces.

sources.quote: כי שבבים - כמו שביבים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word is like שביבים.

sources.quote: ישראל יהיו שבבים, ר"ל בנים שבבים ופראים במעשיהם
sources.says: Malbim says Israel will be wayward, children wild in their deeds.

8:9.headline: Ephraim is like a wild ass, but one that seeks company
8:9.body: פרא is the wild ass. Rashi says Israel became like a wild ass that roams alone. Malbim says a wild ass wanders but hates company. Ephraim wanders too, yet pays for many lovers.

sources.quote: נַעֲשׂוּ כְּפֶרֶא שֶׁהוֹלֵךְ בּוֹדֵד לְעַצְמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says they became like a wild ass that goes off alone by itself.

sources.quote: והוא שונא האהבה והחברה להיות לו רעים רבים, לא כן אפרים
sources.says: Malbim says the wild ass hates closeness and company with many friends, but Ephraim is not like that.

sources.quote: פרא. הוא חמור הבר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the wild donkey.

8:9.headline: A harlot's fee paid for allies
8:9.body: Most read התנו from אתנן, a harlot's fee: Ephraim paid Assyria and Egypt for their love. Radak also hears a deal or condition in it. Rashi brings the Targum's link to תנים, jackals that roam the desert.

sources.quote: התנו. מל׳ אתנן זונה ואמר בל׳ בזיון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from a harlot's fee, said in scorn.

sources.quote: מגזרת אתנן, שהיה כל אחד נותן מנחות של אהבים לשרי האומות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from a harlot's fee: each one gave love gifts to the nations' officials.

sources.quote: לשון תנאי כמו אתנה המה לי אתנן זונה
sources.says: Radak says it is the language of a condition, like 'these are my fee' and 'a harlot's fee'.

sources.quote: יוֹנָתָן תִּרְגֵּם לְשׁוֹן ׳תַּנִּים׳
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum read it from the word for jackals.

8:10.headline: They will tremble, or they will begin
8:10.body: ויחלו can come from חיל, trembling, or from תחלה, beginning. Metzudat Zion reads 'they will tremble' at the king's burden. Radak reads 'they will begin', and Ibn Ezra says grammar allows only that.

sources.quote: ויחלו. מל׳ חיל וחלחלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from trembling and shaking.

sources.quote: ויחלו מעט. ענין תחלה
sources.says: Radak says it means beginning.

sources.quote: ולא יתכן מדרך הדקדוק לפרש: ויחלו רק כמו: וממקדשי תחלו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says grammar allows ויחלו only in the sense of 'begin', as in 'begin at my sanctuary'.

8:11.headline: Altars 'for sin' said twice, meaning two things
8:11.body: The verse says מזבחות לחטא twice. The Targum reads the first as altars that lead to sin and the second as altars that trip them up, and Radak praises this. Malbim says that to Ephraim only the altars to God counted as sin.

sources.quote: ויונתן תירגם לחטא הראשון למחטיא והשני לתקלא ויפה פירש
sources.says: Radak says the Targum renders the first 'to cause sin' and the second 'for a stumbling', and that this is well explained.

sources.quote: רק המזבחות שהיו לו מתחלה לשמים, הם אצלו מזבחות לחטא
sources.says: Malbim says only the altars he first had for Heaven were, in his eyes, altars of sin.

8:12.headline: Written 'the many laws', read 'the great laws'
8:12.body: The written text has רבו, the many laws of my Torah. It is read רבי, the great and weighty parts of my Torah. Radak gives both and says Israel treated them as something foreign.

sources.quote: ופי' הכתוב המצות שרבו בתורתי, ופי' הקרי גדולות ונכבדות מתורתי
sources.says: Radak says the written form means the many commands in my Torah, and the read form means the great and honored parts of my Torah.

sources.quote: רבו. ענין הגדלה ורוממות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means greatness and height.

8:13.headline: Offerings singed in fire, or 'my gifts': a word found only here
8:13.body: הבהבי appears only here. Rashi reads it as offerings singed in the altar fire. Radak reads it as 'my gifts', from יהב, to give. Malbim reads it from להב, flame. The Targum reads offerings taken by force.

sources.quote: זִבְחֵי עוֹלוֹתַי שֶׁהֵם מְהַבְהֲבִים לְפָנַי בָּאֵשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says these are my burnt offerings, singed before me in the fire.

sources.quote: ופי' הבהבי מתנותי
sources.says: Radak says הבהבי means 'my gifts'.

sources.quote: העולות הנתונים ללהב אש
sources.says: Malbim says it means the burnt offerings given to the flame of fire.

sources.quote: דִבְחִין דִמְגַבָּן מִן אוֹנָס
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'offerings collected by force'.

8:14.headline: 'His Maker' means the one who made him great
8:14.body: Israel forgot עשהו, 'the one who made him'. Radak and Metzudat Zion say עשה here means made great, as in 'He made you', and 'who made Moses and Aaron'.

sources.quote: כמו הוא עשך כלומר גדלך וכן אשר עשה את משה ואת אהרן
sources.says: Radak says it is like 'He made you', meaning made you great, and like 'who made Moses and Aaron'.

sources.quote: עשהו. המגדלו ומרוממו כמו הוא עשך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means the one who raised him up and lifted him high.

8:14.headline: Temples for idols, or palaces to hide in
8:14.body: היכל can be a temple or a palace. The Targum reads temples built for idols. Radak also reads palaces built as strongholds, which Israel trusted instead of God.

sources.quote: וּבְנָא הֵיכְלִין לְטַעֲוָתָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'and built temples for idols'.

sources.quote: ויתכן לפרש ויבן היכלות להשגב בהם מפני האויב
sources.says: Radak says it can also mean he built palaces to take shelter in from the enemy.

9:1.headline: גיל is joy over something new and good
9:1.body: Malbim says גיל is the joy of a good thing that has just happened, like success or a find. Metzudat Zion glosses it as plain joy, שמחה.

sources.quote: גיל הוא בדבר טובה המתחדש, כמו הצלחה, מציאה
sources.says: Malbim says גיל is about a good thing that is new, such as success or a find.

sources.quote: גיל. ענין שמחה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says גיל means joy.

9:1.headline: Why threshing floors? Where a prostitute was paid, or idols were served
9:1.body: Rashi says a prostitute was paid in grain at the threshing floor. Radak adds a second reading: people served idols there, thinking the idol gave them the grain.

sources.quote: כְּדֶרֶךְ זוֹנָה שֶׁנּוֹתְנִין לָהּ דָּגָן בַּגֹּרֶן בְּאֶתְנַנָּהּ
sources.says: Rashi says it is like a prostitute, who is given grain at the threshing floor as her fee.

sources.quote: שם בגורן לפי מחשבותם שהנעבד ההוא הוא הנותן התבואה
sources.says: Radak says they worshipped there at the threshing floor, thinking the idol was the one who gave the grain.

9:3.headline: 'The Lord's land': their own country, or Jerusalem?
9:3.body: Rashi reads ארץ ה' as their own land. Radak says it means Jerusalem, and the Targum says 'the land of the Lord's presence'.

sources.quote: לֹא יִתְעַכְּבוּ בְּאַרְצָם
sources.says: Rashi says they will not stay in their land.

sources.quote: לא ישבו בארץ ה'. היא ירושלם
sources.says: Radak says 'the Lord's land' is Jerusalem.

sources.quote: לָא יְתוּבוּן בַּאֲרַע שְׁכִנְתָּא דַייָ
sources.says: The Targum says they will not dwell in the land of the Lord's presence.

9:4.headline: 'Bread of אונים': stolen by force, or eaten in mourning?
9:4.body: Rashi gives two readings: bread taken by force, from און, or bread of mourners, which is unclean. Radak and Ibn Ezra read אונים as mourning, as in 'I did not eat of it in my mourning'.

sources.quote: כְּלֶחֶם גְּזֵלָה הַבָּא עַל יְדֵי כֹּחַ וְאוֹנִים
sources.says: Rashi says it is like bread of robbery that comes by strength and force.

sources.quote: כְּלֶחֶם אֲבֵלִים שֶׁהוּא טָמֵא
sources.says: Rashi gives another reading: like the bread of mourners, which is unclean.

sources.quote: אבלים וכן לא אכלתי באוני
sources.says: Radak says אוני means mourners, as in 'I did not eat of it in my mourning'.

sources.quote: לא אכלתי באוני והוא שם דבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares it to 'I did not eat in my mourning' and says it is a noun.

9:4.headline: Bread 'for their נפש': for themselves, a dead person, or atonement?
9:4.body: Metzudat Zion reads לנפשם as 'for themselves'. Malbim reads נפש as a dead person, as in 'unclean by a soul', and Radak reads it as atonement for their souls.

sources.quote: לנפשם. לעצמם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says לנפשם means 'for themselves'.

sources.quote: לנפש מת, כמו כל טמא לנפש
sources.says: Malbim says it means for a dead person, like 'unclean by a soul'.

sources.quote: כלומר לכפרת נפשם
sources.says: Radak says it means for the atonement of their souls.

9:7.headline: Whose hatred? God's hatred of them, or theirs of the prophet?
9:7.body: Rashi and Radak say משטמה is God's hatred of their deeds. Malbim says it is their hatred of the prophet, which grew once he spoke and rebuked them.

sources.quote: שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שׂוֹנֵא מַעֲשֵׂיכֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it is that the Holy One hates your deeds.

sources.quote: לפיכך רבה משטמת האל יתברך עליכם
sources.says: Radak says that is why God's hatred against you is great.

sources.quote: ועל הנביא גדלה שנאתם יותר אחר שינבא ויוכיח בדבריו
sources.says: Malbim says their hatred of the prophet grew greater after he prophesied and rebuked them.

9:8.headline: A bird-trap on all his ways: who is caught?
9:8.body: Radak says the false prophet is the trap that catches Ephraim, like a bird-trap. Rashi and Malbim say Ephraim sets traps for the true prophet to catch and kill him.

sources.quote: כמו הפח היקוש שלוכד העופות כן ילכדו אפרים בדברי נביאיהם
sources.says: Radak says that, like a bird-trap, Ephraim will be caught by the words of their prophets.

sources.quote: וְלִנְבִיאֵי הָאֱמֶת הֵם טוֹמְנִין פַּחִים לְלָכְדָם
sources.says: Rashi says they hide traps for the true prophets to catch them.

sources.quote: היית מכין פח יקוש על כל דרכיו היית מזמין לו מוקשים ללכדו ולהרגו
sources.says: Malbim says you set a trap on all his ways, preparing snares to catch and kill him.

sources.quote: יקוש. מל׳ מוקש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says יקוש comes from מוקש, 'snare'.

9:8.headline: 'The house of his god': the calves' house, or the Temple?
9:8.body: Radak says it can mean the house of the calves, where the false prophet speaks. It can also mean the Temple, which Rashi ties to the killing of Zechariah there.

sources.quote: נוכל לפרש בית אלהיו בית העגלים שהם אלהיו
sources.says: Radak says we can explain 'his god's house' as the house of the calves, which are his gods.

sources.quote: ונוכל לפרש גם כן בבית אלהיו בבית האל שהוא בית המקדש
sources.says: Radak says we can also explain it as the house of God, the Temple.

sources.quote: בְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הָרְגוּ אֶת זְכַרְיָה
sources.says: Rashi says they killed Zechariah in the Temple.

9:10.headline: 'Shame' is the prophet's name for the idol
9:10.body: בשת means shame, but here it stands for the idol. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say the idol is called this because it shames those who serve it, and Ibn Ezra compares Jeremiah 3:24.

sources.quote: לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שֶׁהִיא בָּשְׁתָּם
sources.says: Rashi says it means the idolatry, which is their shame.

sources.quote: העכו״ם תקרא כן על כי היא לבושת לעובדיה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says idolatry is called this because it is a shame to those who serve it.

sources.quote: כמו: והבושת אכלה יגיע, שם לאליל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like 'the shame consumed the toil' in Jeremiah, a name for an idol.

9:10.headline: 'As they loved': Moab's women, or the way God loved them?
9:10.body: Rashi says it means as they loved the daughters of Moab. Metzudat David and Radak's father say it means as much as God had loved them, so they became that disgusting to Him.

sources.quote: כְּאָהֳבָם. אֶת בְּנוֹת מוֹאָב
sources.says: Rashi says 'as they loved' refers to the daughters of Moab.

sources.quote: כערך אהבתם שאהבתי אותם מתחלה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means to the measure of their love, which I loved them at first.

sources.quote: כמדת האהבה שאהבתים כן היו שקוצים בעיני
sources.says: Radak, giving his father's reading, says that to the measure of love with which I loved them, so were they disgusting in my eyes.

9:10.headline: Grapes in the desert, or 'I found Israel in the desert'?
9:10.body: Ibn Ezra attaches במדבר to the grapes: a desert has no settlement, so whoever finds them is glad. Radak says his father attached it to מצאתי: God found Israel in the desert.

sources.quote: שאין שם יישוב, כל מוצאם ישמח בהן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says there is no settlement there, so everyone who finds them is glad.

sources.quote: פירש טעם במדבר דבק עם מצאתי
sources.says: Radak says his father explained that במדבר attaches to מצאתי.

9:13.headline: 'Planted' means moved from one place to another
9:13.body: Metzudat Zion says שתולה is planting, as in 'a tree planted'. Malbim adds that the verb שתל is used for something moved from place to place, so God moved Ephraim from the desert into a settled land.

sources.quote: ענין נטיעה כמו כעץ שתול
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means planting, like 'a planted tree'.

sources.quote: פעל שתל בא על הנשתל ממקום למקום
sources.says: Malbim says the verb שתל is used of something planted from one place to another.

sources.quote: שאני שתלתי אותו מן המדבר להיות נטוע בנוה
sources.says: Malbim says God planted Ephraim from the desert to be set in a pleasant home.
